title: The Morning a Governor Told James Mwangi to Write His Resignation
dek: In early 1993 Kenya's central bank governor made James Mwangi the price of keeping an insolvent building society open, and Mwangi took a steep pay cut to say yes.

story.event: Leaving Trade Bank to rescue the insolvent Equity Building Society and turn it towards small savers
story.summary: In early 1993, with Equity Building Society found technically insolvent by the Central Bank of Kenya, Governor Eric Kotut made James Mwangi's involvement the condition for keeping it open; Mwangi left his post as group financial controller at Trade Bank for a far smaller salary. Recognising that the society's small, short-term 'mortgage' loans made it a microfinance lender, he turned it towards Kenyans the big banks ignored. It broke even in 1995, became a commercial bank at the end of 2004 and listed in 2006.
paragraphs: In early 1993, by James Mwangi's later account, three men sat in the office of Eric Kotut, governor of the Central Bank of Kenya. Two were founders of Equity Building Society, its chairman Peter Munga and managing director John Mwangi Kagema, come to plead against its closure. They had brought Mwangi, 31, group financial controller at Trade Bank and one of the society's three largest depositors; he had put his savings into it in 1992 at a founder's urging.

The figures were bad. The regulator had found the society, set up in 1984 for farmers and traders, technically insolvent: more than half its loans were not being repaid, its liquidity was 5.8 per cent against a legal minimum of 20, and accumulated losses exceeded Sh30 million. A large depositor had complained that it was paying its running costs from customers' money. Kotut did not believe its managers could turn it round, and his condition for keeping it open was Mwangi. "The governor pushed his writing pad to me and told me to write my resignation," Mwangi recalled.

He said he felt he could not abandon the two founders. The cost was concrete. His monthly pay, he told the Harvard professor Ranjay Gulati, fell from Sh360,000 to Sh60,000; a 2019 profile put the cut at 94 per cent. "My wife was troubled, I was newly wedded and we had just got our firstborn son," he said.

What he found, he later explained, was a society whose "mortgages" were small, short-term and not spent on houses. It was already a microfinance lender. He leaned into that: many small loans spread the risk, and the market would be the people big banks ignored, like his mother, who had no account. "My vision was to build a bank for my mother," he said. Through the mid-1990s its managers and staff went out to the market places to sell accounts.

Trade Bank itself was shut by the regulator before the end of 1993. Equity made a small operating profit in 1995, the year Mwangi formally became finance director. It became a commercial bank at the end of 2004 and listed in Nairobi in 2006, with roughly a million deposit customers.

quote.text: The benefits of a sea voyage are innumerable; but if thou seekest for safety, it is to be found only on shore.
quote.locator: Chapter I, "Of the Customs of Kings", Story XVI
quote.source_title: The Persian Literature, Volume 2 (The Gulistan, tr. James Ross), Project Gutenberg eBook #13060
quote.connection: Saadi gives this advice to a friend with a large family and "some small skill in the science of accounts", who ignores it, takes a royal post, rises high and then falls. Mwangi, an accountant with a newborn son, also left the shore. It went the other way for him, which does not prove Saadi wrong.

reflection: Saadi's caution is not foolish. Mwangi had a newborn son, a salary that kept a household and, by his own account, no family money behind him, and he gave up most of that salary for an institution the regulator had already judged insolvent. That it worked does not mean the risk was small, and his wife's worry was not a failure of nerve. It was accurate.

If you are weighing your own version of this, the useful question is not whether you are brave enough. It is who else is carrying the cost with you, and whether they have had a real say. A decision made at a governor's desk still lands at home.
invitation: Ask the person who shares your household which part of your work worries them most, and listen to the whole answer before you explain or reassure.

sources.title: The day CBK governor almost shut down Equity bank
sources.supports: Mwangi's account, given on Ranjay Gulati's Deep Purpose podcast, of the early-1993 meeting in Governor Eric Kotut's office with Peter Munga and John Mwangi Kagema; Mwangi aged 31, group financial controller at Trade Bank and one of the top three depositors; a major depositor's complaint that deposits were funding operations; Kotut's condition that Mwangi lead the restructuring; 'The governor pushed his writing pad to me and told me to write my resignation'; Kotut telephoning Trade Bank's managing director; Mwangi's feeling that he could not abandon the founders; monthly pay falling from Sh360,000 to Sh60,000; 'My wife was troubled, I was newly wedded and we had just got our firstborn son'; society founded in 1984 for rural farmers and merchants; 1993 deposits of Sh31 million and loans of Sh12 million; accumulated losses of Sh35 million; CBK's end-1992 finding of technical insolvency, liquidity of 5.8% against 20%, non-performing loans of 54%; Trade Bank shut by the CBK before the end of 1993; conversion to a commercial bank at the end of 2004 and listing in 2006.

sources.title: The bank that turned social innovation into profit
sources.publisher: Think:Act Magazine, Roland Berger (Patrick Gathara, 14 November 2019)
sources.supports: Mwangi's career at PwC, Ernst & Young and Trade Bank, where he became group financial controller; investing his savings in the society in 1992 at a founder's urging; leaving Trade Bank for a directorship at the failing society with a 94% pay cut (dated 1994 in this profile); the Central Bank of Kenya declaring it technically insolvent; his realisation that its 'mortgage loans' were small, short-term and not used for housing, so that it was really in microfinance; spreading risk through many small loans; 'My mother didn't have a bank account' and 'my vision was to build a bank for my mother'; 14 million customers by 2019.

sources.title: A Market-led Revolution: Equity Bank's Continuing Story (March 2007)
sources.publisher: MicroSave (Graham A. N. Wright and David Cracknell)
sources.supports: Paper (PDF linked from this page): CBK confirmation that the society was technically insolvent, with non-performing loans of 54% of the portfolio, accumulated losses of KSh 33 million against paid-up capital of KSh 3 million and liquidity of 5.8% against a required 20%; a capital injection allowing it to continue; 1993 migration to focus exclusively on microfinance; Mwangi depositing significant funds and bringing other depositors; staff selling in the market places from 1993 to 1997, with clients opening accounts across branch managers' desks; a small operating profit (break-even) in 1995; Mwangi moving from consultant to finance director and board member in 1995; conversion to a bank on 1 January 2005; listing in August 2006; about one million deposit clients by 2006.

sources.title: The Case of Equity Bank (Stanford Graduate School of Business case, 2007)
sources.supports: By 1993 non-performing loans of 54%, accumulated losses of KSh 33 million and liquidity of 5.8% against a 20% minimum; the CBK finding of technical insolvency (dated 1994 in this case); Mwangi's 1992 deposit at a founder's urging; joining as finance director in 1995 after Ernst & Young and Trade Bank; the focus on the unbanked, accounts opened with only a national ID; listing on the Nairobi Stock Exchange in August 2006.

sources.title: Equity Bank (A), case E260
sources.supports: Case summary: the CBK found Equity Building Society technically insolvent, citing poor management and inadequate board supervision; officials agreed to overhaul strategy and operations to avoid dissolution; Mwangi first involved in 1992 when he deposited his savings, joining as finance director in 1995 and becoming CEO in 2004; the focus on Kenya's unbanked.

sources.title: Our troubled history made us stronger, says Equity CEO
sources.supports: Mwangi recalling the low point when Equity Building Society was declared technically insolvent by the regulator after the 1993 difficulties, and the strategy of drawing savings of the unbanked from under their mattresses.

cross_checks.claim: Mwangi left his post as group financial controller at Trade Bank, taking a steep pay cut, to help rescue the insolvent Equity Building Society.
The Central Bank of Kenya found the society technically insolvent, with non-performing loans of 54% and liquidity of 5.8% against a required 20%.
Accumulated losses exceeded Sh30 million (KSh 33 million in MicroSave and Stanford; Sh35 million in Business Daily).
Mwangi had put his savings into the society in 1992 at a founder's urging.
The society was refocused on microfinance and the unbanked.
Mwangi formally became finance director in 1995.
Equity became a commercial bank at the end of 2004 and listed in Nairobi in 2006.

research_notes: Dates disagree. The slate said 1994. Mwangi's own recollection (Business Daily, 2024, from the Deep Purpose podcast) puts the meeting with Governor Eric Kotut in early 1993, which fits Kotut's tenure and Trade Bank's closure that year; MicroSave records his recruitment in 1993, first as a consultant; Roland Berger (2019) dates his move from Trade Bank to 1994; Stanford and MicroSave both say he formally became finance director in 1995. The story follows Mwangi's dating for the meeting and gives 1995 for the formal appointment. The insolvency finding is dated end-1992 (Business Daily), 1992/3 and 1993 (MicroSave) and 1994 (Stanford); the story gives no date for it. Pay: Business Daily, from Mwangi's podcast account, gives Sh360,000 falling to Sh60,000 a month (about an 83% cut); Roland Berger says 94%. The story gives both with attribution. Losses: MicroSave and Stanford say accumulated losses of KSh 33 million (MicroSave's annex gives 32-and-a-fraction million); Business Daily says Sh35 million; the story uses the conservative 'more than Sh30 million'. Deposit base: Roland Berger says the society had nearly 3,000 accounts with three depositors holding 85% of deposits, while MicroSave's chart shows about 12,000 deposit clients in 1994; the story does not give an account count. Customers in 2006: MicroSave's text says 'nearly a million' and its chart 1,018,000; the story says roughly a million. Roland Berger also says Equity became a commercial bank in 2007, which conflicts with MicroSave and Business Daily (end of 2004); the story uses end of 2004. The quotation about his mother comes from Roland Berger; the Star (13 November 2025) independently reports Mwangi linking his banking philosophy to his mother's treatment at a bank. Funding is 'mixed': a member-owned society recapitalised in 1993, later taking a MESP loan and grant and a 2002 AfriCap equity investment (MicroSave). The MicroSave landing page links the full PDF (https://www.microsave.net/wp-content/uploads/2007/03/A_Market_led_Revolution_Equity_Bank_s_Continuing_Story.pdf). African Business's 2012 profile returned 403 and was not used. In Saadi's story the narrator gives this advice, the friend rejects it, and Saadi then helps him to a post anyway; the later fall follows a false accusation rather than incompetence.
